at pakke.explanation: "At pakke" means to pack, like a suitcase or a bag. "Jeg pakker min kuffert" means "I pack my suitcase". It also means to wrap, as in "pakke en gave ind" (wrap a present). A parcel is "en pakke", so the thing and the action look the same.

sentence.en: I am packing my suitcase tonight.

at prøve.explanation: "At prøve" means to try, and also to test or to try on: "Jeg prøver at lære dansk" (I am trying to learn Danish). In a shop you "prøver" clothes. Notice the little word "at" after it before another action word. A test or an exam is also called "en prøve".

sentence.en: I am trying to speak Danish.

at prøve tøj.explanation: "At prøve tøj" means to try on clothes in a shop. "At prøve" on its own means to try or to test. You can say "Må jeg prøve den?" (May I try it on?). The fitting room is "prøverummet", so the two words go together.

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **prøve tøj** i butikken.
sentence.en: I would like to try on clothes in the shop.

en pakke.explanation: "Pakke" means a package or parcel that you send or receive, and also a packet, like "en pakke cigaretter" or "en pakke smør". The word "at pakke" means to pack. Use it when you talk about mail: "Der er kommet en pakke" (A parcel has arrived).

sentence.da: Der er kommet **en pakke** til dig.
sentence.en: A package has come for you.

en pandekage.explanation: "En pandekage" is a pancake, an en-word. It is made of "pande" (a pan) and "kage" (cake). Danish pancakes are thin, like crepes, and are often eaten with jam or sugar and rolled up. Several are "pandekager", and a pancake pan is "en pande".

sentence.en: My mother makes pancakes on Sundays.

en paraply.explanation: "Paraply" is an umbrella, said pa-ra-PLY. Since Danish weather changes a lot, Danes often say "Tag en paraply med" (Take an umbrella with you). The word ends in -y but the plural just adds -er: "paraplyer".

sentence.en: Take an umbrella with you.

en park.explanation: En park is a park, a green public area in a town where people walk, play and relax. It looks just like the English word, and you say "i parken" for "in the park". Be careful: the similar-looking "at parkere" means to park a car. The word is an en-word, so "the park" is "parken".

sentence.en: The children are playing in the park.

en patient.explanation: "En patient" is a patient, a person getting medical care. It is an en-word. It is spelled like the English word but the "ti" sounds like "tsi", so it says "pa-tsi-ent". It is the person you find at "et sygehus" or "en klinik".

sentence.en: The doctor talks with the patient.

en pause.explanation: "En pause" means a break or a pause, for example at work or school. It is an en-word. "At holde pause" means to take a break, and "frokostpause" is a lunch break. For a short coffee break you may hear "en kaffepause".

sentence.en: We take a break at ten o'clock.

en pen.explanation: "En pen" is a pen. It is an en-word, and the word for more than one is "penne". Do not confuse it with the Danish word "pæn", which means nice or pretty, and is spelled with an "æ". A ballpoint pen is often called "en kuglepen".

sentence.en: I write with a pen.

en perron.explanation: "Perron" is the platform at a train station where you wait for the train. You will hear "Toget kører fra perron 3" (The train leaves from platform 3). In English one would say "platform", but Danish uses the French-style word "perron". It is an en-word.

sentence.en: The train leaves from platform two.

en person.explanation: "En person" is a person, and it is an en-word. The plural is "personer". In restaurants or when booking you say "et bord til to personer" (a table for two people). For people in general, the more everyday word is "mennesker".

sentence.en: There are three people in the car.

en pige.explanation: "En pige" is a girl. It is an en-word. The plural "piger" is regular. Be careful: "pige" can also be used for a girlfriend, or a young woman, but for a grown woman "en kvinde" is safer. Its pair is "en dreng" (a boy).

sentence.da: Den lille **pige** har en rød kjole.
sentence.en: The little girl has a red dress.

en pille.explanation: "En pille" is a pill or tablet. It is an en-word. You swallow it: "at tage en pille" (to take a pill). A similar word is "en tablet". Be careful: "pillen" can also mean the birth control pill, depending on context.

sentence.da: Tag en **pille** to gange om dagen.
sentence.en: Take one pill twice a day.

en pingvin.explanation: "En pingvin" is a penguin, an en-word. It is spelled with "v", not "gu" as in English. The penguin is a bird that lives in cold places and swims well. Children love seeing penguins at the zoo.

sentence.en: The penguin swims in the water.

en pizza.explanation: "En pizza" is a pizza, and it is an en-word. In Denmark pizza is very popular, and you can order one to take away with "en pizza til at tage med". The plural is "pizzaer", and you say "pizzaen" when you mean a specific one.

sentence.en: We are ordering a pizza tonight.

en plads.explanation: "En plads" means a seat, a space or room for something, and also a town square. It is an en-word, and the plural is "pladser". On a train or in a cinema, "en plads" is your seat. "Er der plads?" means "Is there room?", and "Der er ikke mere plads" means there is no more room.

sentence.en: Is there room for me?

en plan.explanation: "En plan" is a plan, and it is an en-word. The plural is "planer". A common question is "Har du planer i weekenden?" (Do you have plans this weekend?). The verb is "at planlægge", to plan. A schedule can also be "en køreplan" for buses.

sentence.da: Hvad er din **plan** for i dag?
sentence.en: What is your plan for today?

en plastikpose.explanation: "En plastikpose" is a plastic bag, and it is an en-word. It is built from "plastik" (plastic) and "en pose" (a bag). In shops you may hear "Vil du have en pose?" (Do you want a bag?). In Denmark you usually pay for them, so many people bring their own "bæretaske" or "net".

sentence.en: I need a plastic bag.

en politistation.explanation: "En politistation" is a police station, built from "politi" and "station". It is an en-word. If you lose something or need to report a theft, you go there. In an emergency, call 112 rather than going in person. Say "på politistationen" for "at the police station".

sentence.en: Where is the police station?

en portion.explanation: "En portion" is a portion or a serving, such as one person's share of food. It is an en-word. In restaurants you may hear "en lille portion" (a small portion) or "en stor portion" (a large one). The word looks like English, but the stress is at the end, "por-ti-ON".

sentence.en: Can I have a large portion?

en pose.explanation: "Pose" is a soft bag made of plastic or paper, like a shopping bag from a shop. A harder bag you carry, such as a handbag, is "en taske". In Danish shops you will hear "Skal du have en pose?" (Do you want a bag?). The two words are easy to mix up, so link "pose" with shops and "taske" with carrying.

sentence.en: Do you want a bag?

en pris.explanation: En pris is a price, what something costs. It is an en-word, so "the price" is "prisen". The same word also means a prize or award, so the meaning comes from the situation: "en pris på tyve kroner" is a price, while "at vinde en pris" is to win a prize. A common question in shops is "Hvad er prisen?".

sentence.en: What is the price?

en pude.explanation: "En pude" is a pillow or a cushion, and it is an en-word. It works for the one on a bed ("en hovedpude", a head pillow) and for a cushion on a sofa. At a hotel you can ask for an extra one: "kan jeg få en ekstra pude?".

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en ekstra **pude**.
sentence.en: I would like an extra pillow.

en pung.explanation: "En pung" is a small wallet or purse for coins and notes. It is an everyday word, and you will often hear "Jeg har glemt min pung" (I have forgotten my wallet). "En tegnebog" means almost the same thing and is a slightly more formal word. Both are used, but "pung" is more common in speech.

sentence.en: Where is my wallet?

en pyjamas.explanation: "En pyjamas" means pajamas, and in Danish it is a single en-word, so you say "en pyjamas", not a plural. You wear it to sleep, and it is also used for lazy days at home. Notice the spelling with a y and a j, which is different from English. Add "en" to get "pyjamassen" (the pajamas).

sentence.en: The children are wearing pajamas.

en pære.explanation: "En pære" is a pear, an en-word. The same word is also used for a light bulb, "en pære", so the meaning depends on what you are talking about. Context makes it clear: "en saftig pære" is a juicy pear, while "en ny pære" is probably a new bulb.

sentence.da: Jeg har købt tre **pærer** på markedet.
sentence.en: I bought three pears at the market.

en pølse.explanation: "En pølse" is a sausage. Danes love hot dogs, called "en hotdog" or "en pølse i brød". You can buy them at a "pølsevogn", a sausage stand on the street. The plural is "pølser".

sentence.en: I would like a sausage.

et par.explanation: "Et par" means a pair, such as "et par sko" (a pair of shoes), and also "a few": "et par dage" means a couple of days. It is an et-word. A romantic couple is also "et par". Note that when it means "a few", you do not add -er to the next word, you say "et par minutter".

sentence.en: I will stay here for a couple of days.

et par jeans.explanation: "Et par jeans" means a pair of jeans. "Et par" is "a pair", and "jeans" is used just like in English, always with more than one. You can also just say "jeans": "Jeg har jeans på". The pronunciation is close to English.

sentence.en: I have bought a pair of jeans.

et pas.explanation: "Pas" is a passport, the document you show at the border. It is an et-word and, with a number, it stays the same: "to pas". Say "Har du dit pas?" before every trip. Be careful: it is also the start of other words like "at passe" (to fit, to look after).

sentence.en: Do you have your passport?

et plaster.explanation: "Et plaster" is a band-aid, a small sticky bandage you put on a cut. It is an et-word. You say "at sætte et plaster på" (to put a band-aid on). You can buy them at a pharmacy ("et apotek") or in most supermarkets.

sentence.en: I need a band-aid.

et postkontor.explanation: "Et postkontor" is a post office, where you send letters and parcels. It is built from "post" (mail) and "kontor" (office), and it is an et-word. In Denmark many post services now sit inside shops, so you may also hear "et posthus". Take your parcel with you and ask at the counter.

sentence.en: When does the post office open?

et postkort.explanation: "Et postkort" is a postcard, and it is an et-word. The plural is the same as the singular: "to postkort" is two postcards. It is built from "post" (mail) and "kort" (card). People send them on holiday, with "Hilsen fra ..." (Greetings from ...) written on them.

sentence.en: I am sending a postcard home.

et problem.explanation: "Et problem" is a problem, and it is an et-word. The plural is "problemer". Danes often say "Det er ikke noget problem" (It is no problem) or just "Ikke noget problem" to be relaxed about something. "Hvad er problemet?" means "What is the problem?".

sentence.en: There is a problem with the car.

et prøverum.explanation: "Et prøverum" is the small room in a clothing shop where you try on clothes. It comes from "at prøve" (to try) and "et rum" (a room). The plural is the same as the single word, "prøverum". In a shop you can ask "Hvor er prøverummet?" (Where is the fitting room?).

sentence.en: Where is the fitting room?

forms.en: There is a deposit on the bottle

pant.explanation: "Pant" is the deposit you pay on bottles and cans in Denmark. You get the money back when you return the empty bottle at a machine in the shop. It is an et-word, and you say "pantet" for the deposit. Learn it early, since you see it on bottles all the time and the word is a part of daily life.

sentence.en: I am going to return deposit bottles at the shop.

papir.explanation: "Papir" means paper, the material you write or print on. It is an et-word, so "the paper" is "papiret". You say "et stykke papir" for one sheet. In the plural, "papirer" often means documents or official papers, for example at a border or a hotel.

sentence.da: Jeg har brug for et stykke **papir**.
sentence.en: I need a piece of paper.

pas på.explanation: "Pas på" means "watch out" or "be careful". It is both a warning shouted in an emergency and a calm reminder, like "pas på, det er varmt". It also means "look after": "pas på børnene" is "look after the children". Tone tells you which one is meant.

sentence.en: Watch out, the floor is wet!

forms.da: Pas på dig selv i trafikken.
forms.en: Look after yourself in the traffic.

pas på dig selv.explanation: "Pas på dig selv" is a warm way to say goodbye, like "take care of yourself". It is often said to someone going on a trip, feeling ill, or just heading home. The words "dig selv" mean "yourself". If you talk to several people, say "pas på jer selv".

sentence.en: Goodbye, and take care of yourself!

pasta.explanation: "Pasta" means pasta, and it is an en-word, so "the pasta" is "pastaen". It is spelled and said much like in English. It needs no "a" in front: "Jeg laver pasta". It is a very common weekday dinner in Denmark.

sentence.en: I am making pasta for dinner.

peber.explanation: "Peber" is pepper, the spice you put on food. It is almost always used without "en" or "et", for example "salt og peber" (salt and pepper). It is also part of other words, such as "peberfrugt" (bell pepper), which is a vegetable and not the same thing as the spice.

sentence.en: I add a little salt and pepper.

penge.explanation: Penge is the word for money, and it only exists in the "more than one" form. That means you never put "en" or "et" in front of it, and you do not say "a money". "The money" is "pengene". To talk about one single coin or note, use words like "en mønt" or "en seddel". A typical phrase is "Jeg har ingen penge" (I have no money).

sentence.en: I do not have much money.

perfekt.explanation: "Perfekt" means perfect, just like in English. It does not change with et-words ("et perfekt svar"), and it adds an "e" with more than one ("perfekte dage"). Alone it works as an exclamation: "Perfekt!" means "Great, that works!".

sentence.en: It is the perfect gift.

pludselig.explanation: "Pludselig" means suddenly in everyday speech: "Pludselig kom han ind" (Suddenly he came in). "Lige pludselig" adds a bit of stress, like "all of a sudden". You can also use it to describe things: "en pludselig lyd" (a sudden sound). It is a good word for telling stories.

sentence.en: Suddenly it began to rain.

polen.explanation: "Polen" is Poland. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Polen" means "in Poland" and "til Polen" means "to Poland". A person is "en polak" and the language is "polsk". Many Polish people live and work in Denmark.

sentence.en: My colleague comes from Poland.

politi.explanation: "Politi" means the police, and it is an et-word. Most of the time you say "politiet" (the police) with "the" on the end. Danish treats it as one thing, so you say "politiet er her" (the police is here). A single officer is "en politibetjent", and the emergency number is 112.

sentence.en: The police will come in five minutes.

polsk.explanation: "Polsk" means Polish. It describes things from Poland and is also the name of the language. It is written with a small letter and gets no extra -t before an et-word. The English word "polish" for shoe polish is a different word and has nothing to do with it.

sentence.da: Min nabo kommer fra Polen og taler **polsk**.
sentence.en: My neighbour comes from Poland and speaks Polish.

pommes frites.explanation: "Pommes frites" are French fries, and the word is said in a French-like way. It is plural and has no "en" or "et". You often hear the short form "pommes", and people may say "fritter" too. Burger places ask "vil du have pommes frites til?" (do you want fries with that?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have **pommes frites** og ketchup.
sentence.en: I would like fries and ketchup.

post.explanation: "Post" is the mail, meaning the letters and parcels that arrive, and it is also the postal service. It is an en-word and it has no plural, so you say "Der er post til dig" (There is mail for you). The person who brings it is "postbudet", and the office is "postkontoret".

sentence.en: Have you got the mail?

præcis.explanation: "Præcis" means exactly or precisely, and it is used for time, amounts and details. As a one-word answer, "Præcis!" means "Exactly!" or "That's right!", which is very handy in conversation. For a rough amount, use "cirka" instead.

sentence.en: The train comes exactly at eight o'clock.

på.explanation: "På" means on, and also at in many fixed phrases: "på arbejde" (at work), "på ferie" (on holiday), "på dansk" (in Danish). These are best learned as whole phrases. It is also used with islands and many open places: "på Fyn", "på gaden".

sentence.en: The phone is on the table.

på gensyn.explanation: "På gensyn" means "until we see each other again" and is a polite, slightly formal goodbye. It is common in shops, on the phone and at work. With friends, "vi ses" is more usual. Both mean you hope to meet again.

sentence.en: Thanks for the visit. See you again!

på tilbud.explanation: "På tilbud" means on sale, with a lower price for a short time. You see it on shop signs, often next to a red price. It comes from "et tilbud" (an offer). It is a small phrase, so it does not change, whatever it is about.

sentence.da: Kaffen er **på tilbud** i denne uge.
sentence.en: The coffee is on sale this week.

forms.en: The bus is on its way.

på vej.explanation: Means "on the way" and is used for both coming and going. Say "jeg er på vej" when you are travelling toward a place. Add the place after it, like "på vej hjem" (on the way home) or "på vej til arbejde" (on the way to work). It is very handy in text messages.

sentence.en: I'm on my way to school.

påske.explanation: "Påske" means Easter. It is an en-word, but you usually use it with no "en": "til påske" (at Easter) and "i påsken" (during Easter). The greeting is "Glædelig påske!". Easter is a long holiday in Denmark, with days off on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Monday.

sentence.en: We are on holiday at Easter.

pæn.explanation: "Pæn" means nice-looking, neat or tidy. It is used for people and things that look good in a simple way, for clean and tidy rooms, and for polite behaviour: "vær pæn" means be well-behaved. Add "t" for et-words ("et pænt værelse") and "-e" for more than one. "Pænt" on its own is a common reply meaning "nicely" or "pretty well".

sentence.da: Du ser meget **pæn** ud i dag.
sentence.en: You look very nice today.
